strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem in LLM alignment—the faithfulness of chain-of-thought explanations under reward model optimization
Clear problem formulation with intuitive motivation; the concept of 'CoT hacking' is well-articulated
Rigorous experimental design with controlled settings, multiple reward models, multiple decoding strategies, and proper statistical reporting (3 seeds, standard deviations)
Convincing empirical evidence that reward models actively promote CoT hacking, demonstrated through both BoN and DPO
Practical solution that is simple to implement and requires no changes to generation strategies
Good reproducibility with detailed prompts, experimental procedures, and comprehensive appendices
Novel observation that preference optimization can degrade explanation faithfulness despite improving task performance
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope: only two artificial, heavily controlled settings tested; single base model (LLama-3.1-8B-IT); unclear generalization to realistic scenarios with subtle or implicit protected features
Task-specific approach requiring manual identification of protected features; impractical for real-world deployment without domain-specific configuration
Relies on Eval LLM with F1 score of only 0.65 for BiasQA positive class, introducing significant noise into evaluation; no human evaluation of actual CoT faithfulness
Inconsistent and modest improvements, especially for DPO (Math Book: 22.8±0.6 → 22.8±0.6; BiasQA: 13.7% → 12.3% unfaithful), with no analysis of why results differ between BoN and DPO
Simplistic causal attribution methodology (binary comparison of feature present/absent); more sophisticated causal approaches unexplored
Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing counterfactual methods and appends disclaimer text; contribution is mainly empirical validation
No computational cost analysis for counterfactual generation; no discussion of trade-offs between faithfulness and task performance
Missing comparison with alternative solutions (e.g., reward model ensembles, training RMs with interpretability data, post-hoc monitoring)
Unclear whether findings generalize to complex reasoning tasks; only tested on math word problems and pronoun resolution
No statistical significance testing; some comparisons show large standard deviations relative to effect sizes

strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: reward hacking in LLM explanations during alignment
Clear and compelling problem motivation with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2)
Rigorous empirical methodology with proper counterfactual evaluation across two reward models
Convincing demonstration that reward models do promote CoT hacking across multiple settings
Comprehensive experimental details supporting reproducibility
Honest reporting of results including weaker DPO outcomes
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: only two highly artificial, toy settings (Math Book, BiasQA) with simple binary protected features and explicit instructions, raising serious questions about generalizability to realistic alignment scenarios

Proposed solution is task-specific and impractical: requires knowing protected features beforehand, relies on fragile counterfactual generation, and uses an unreliable Eval LLM with F1 as low as 0.65 for BiasQA
Mixed and marginal results: DPO improvements are weak (2.4 percentage points for Math Book), BoN is more expensive, and improvements often fall within standard deviations

Limited technical novelty: counterfactual evaluation is not new (Turpin et al. 2024, Atanasova et al. 2023), and the solution (appending disclaimer text) is straightforward, not a novel algorithmic contribution

Incomplete analysis: no ablation studies explaining RMC vs RMD differences, no comparison with simpler alternatives or other CoT faithfulness methods, insufficient investigation of why DPO is much less effective than BoN
Methodological concerns: circular definition of unfaithfulness, reliance on another LLM for evaluation, no computational cost analysis for counterfactual generation, no formal significance testing
Scalability issues: approach requires task-specific protected features and cannot generalize to unknown forms of reward hacking or multiple conflicting objectives
Practical concerns about false security: penalizing one feature may not address hidden use of other features; unclear how this scales beyond binary protected attributes

strengths: Identifies an important and previously understudied failure mode ('CoT hacking') in LLM preference optimization where reward models inadvertently encourage unfaithful explanations
Clear problem demonstration through well-designed controlled experiments with effective use of original/counterfactual comparisons to isolate causal effects
Comprehensive experimental evaluation covering both inference-time (BoN) and training-time (DPO) approaches, with multiple reward models, metrics, and seeds reported
Creative and practical solution using causal attribution from counterfactuals to augment reward model inputs; principled approach to detecting unfaithful explanations
Strong results on BiasQA setting: augmented RMs reduce stereotype rate while closing the fidelity gap by 71% in some configurations
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, public datasets, available models, and methodological transparency
Clear presentation with effective figures and logical flow from motivation through solution to evaluation
weaknesses: Limited scope with only two controlled, somewhat artificial settings; unclear generalizability to realistic domains with implicit, continuous, or correlated features
Method requires knowing and generating counterfactuals for the protected feature in advance, which is often infeasible in practice; computational costs of counterfactual generation not discussed
Modest improvements in several cases: only 2.4 percentage points for Math Book with DPO (Table 1); RMD sometimes underperforms baseline
Dependence on Eval LLM for acknowledgment detection with imperfect F1 scores (0.65 for BiasQA positive labels), introducing measurement error that could affect conclusions
Limited technical novelty: counterfactual explanations are standard; core contribution is appending text disclaimers to reward model inputs rather than a sophisticated mechanism
Insufficient guidance on strategy selection: RMC outperforms RMD empirically but paper provides limited intuition about when each is appropriate beyond these specific settings

Incomplete analysis of failure modes: no discussion of what happens with multiple causally-relevant features, counterfactual corruption of other input properties, or when protected features are legitimately needed
Practical applicability unclear: real-world LLMs rarely have clearly-defined protected features; per-example counterfactual generation may be computationally prohibitive at scale

strengths: Identifies important, timely problem of how preference optimization can promote unfaithful CoT explanations during alignment
Clear, well-motivated problem formulation with intuitive examples (Math Book and BiasQA settings)
Rigorous experimental design with thorough evaluation: multiple reward models, two alignment methods (BoN and DPO), multiple decoding strategies, and multiple LLM generators
Comprehensive evidence of problem: consistent demonstration across settings showing reward models drive CoT hacking (e.g., accuracy +18.4pp, acknowledgment -1.0pp)
Practical solution with low computational overhead—no retraining required, only additional sampling
Extensive supplementary materials including ablation studies, generalization tests, and implementation details enabling reproducibility
Well-organized writing that clearly communicates the problem and approach
weaknesses: Severely limited generalization: only 2 controlled settings with explicit instructions; unclear applicability to real-world scenarios without such instructions
Preliminary generalization to CodeMMLU (Table 4) shows mixed results with effectiveness varying across model combinations
Method depends on task-specific high-quality counterfactuals; creating counterfactuals is difficult and non-trivial, limiting practical applicability
Inconsistent effectiveness: DPO on Math Book (greedy) shows RMC reduces gap by only 2.4pp vs. 41% for BoN; insufficient analysis of failure modes
Eval LLM reliability issues: BiasQA evaluation shows F1=0.75 (vs. F1=0.93 for Math Book) with noted false positives; noise undermines confidence in acknowledgment measurements
Low absolute acknowledgment rates even in 'successful' cases (<20% in Table 1); unclear if improvements reflect genuine understanding or surface-level adjustments
Insufficient mechanistic understanding: why does causal attribution change reward model priorities? Why does RMC consistently outperform RMD? Limited exploration of these questions
Strategy C (RMC) requires knowing which predictions align with cues (meta-knowledge not always available), limiting applicability compared to Strategy D
No formal statistical significance testing despite multiple model combinations; some reported improvements fall within measurement noise margins
Dense presentation of results (Figure 4) and notation (RM, RMD, RMC) could be clearer; key details relegated to appendices

strengths: Addresses an important and timely safety problem: reward models inadvertently promoting unfaithful explanations (CoT hacking)
Clear empirical demonstration of the problem in controlled settings with compelling examples (Figure 1b, 4)
Principled methodological approach using counterfactual interventions to measure causal influence
Comprehensive experiments within scope: multiple RMs, LLMs, decoding strategies, with proper error reporting
Practical solution with minimal computational overhead requiring no RM/LLM retraining
Extensive appendices supporting reproducibility with prompts, implementation details, and additional results
weaknesses: Critical limitation: evaluation restricted to only two highly artificial, controlled settings (Math Book, BiasQA); generalization to realistic scenarios (distribution shift, adversarial inputs) is undemonstrated; brief CodeMMLU generalization study (Appendix F) shows mixed results

Mixed and often modest DPO results: Math Book + SK-GEMMA-27B shows only 2.4 pp improvement; RMD sometimes underperforms baseline; strong improvements seen only in BoN (inference-time), not training-time alignment

Fundamental dependence on task-specific, high-quality counterfactuals; for realistic protected attributes (subtle biases, high-dimensional features), counterfactual generation is intractable; no systematic evaluation of counterfactual quality

Eval LLM used for acknowledgment detection has non-trivial error rates (F1=0.75 for BiasQA); during training, RMD/RMC use noisy signals rather than actual acknowledgments; no ablation on impact of this noise

Lacks theoretical justification for why appending acknowledgment disclaimers to RM input causally influences CoT generation; mechanism by which augmented rewards reduce hacking is unclear; Appendix Figure 7 shows RMALL largely ineffective but implications unexplored

Limited novelty: counterfactual-based explanation evaluation exists in prior work; applying known techniques to RM inputs is incremental; parallel work (Turpin et al. 2025) proposes similar approaches
Missing key comparisons: no baselines for training faithfulness before alignment, no comparison to ensemble or reward shaping alternatives, insufficient engagement with parallel work

Artificial experimental design: instructions to 'not use' protected features lack realism; both settings appear engineered to fit the method; strategy C requires task-specific knowledge of what counts as 'cued'
Presentation issues: dense writing obscures key findings; DPO's weaker results somewhat buried; distinction between strategies D and C underexplained; notation introduced late
Practical applicability concerns: choosing RMD vs. RMC requires domain-specific tuning; limited evidence the method generalizes beyond toy settings

strengths: Identifies and clearly motivates an important problem: reward models can inadvertently incentivize unfaithful chain-of-thought explanations, creating a gap between LLM decisions and their explanations
Proposes a novel application of causal attribution: augmenting reward model inputs with counterfactual signals to detect CoT hacking

Comprehensive experimental design spanning two distinct problem settings, multiple LLMs and reward models, both inference and training-time methods, with thorough ablations and multiple evaluation metrics
Methodologically sound use of counterfactuals to measure model reliance, with principled strategies (D and C) for incorporating faithfulness signals
Results are consistent across different models, reward models, and decoding strategies, suggesting robustness within tested scope
Clear and well-structured presentation with effective motivation (Figure 1) and good reproducibility (detailed appendices, training details)
Demonstrates that standard RM-guided alignment (BoN, DPO) can exacerbate CoT hacking across both settings
weaknesses: Severely limited scope: experiments restricted to two controlled, artificial settings with explicit, easily-manipulable protected features (solution in math book, profession in pronoun task); unclear how approach generalizes to real-world alignment problems with subtle implicit protected attributes

Approach critically depends on high-quality counterfactual examples, which are task-specific and difficult to generate; for subtle/implicit biases the problem becomes much harder; preliminary generalization results (Appendix F) on CodeMMLU are mixed and inconclusive
Modest and inconsistent improvements: DPO Math Book (greedy) shows only 2.4pp gap reduction; some improvements may be within noise margins; practical significance of gains is unclear

Acknowledgment detection via Eval LLM has quality issues: F1=0.75 and accuracy=0.79 on BiasQA; explicit acknowledgment of false positives, extrapolation errors, and ambiguity; this noise propagates into faithfulness detection
During DPO training, disclaimers are added without using Eval LLM (for efficiency), potentially introducing false positives and degrading preference data; impact of this approximation is not analyzed
Limited novelty in core technique: counterfactual-based faithfulness evaluation is established; the main contribution is applying it to RM augmentation during alignment, which is somewhat incremental
Insufficient analysis of why RMC consistently outperforms RMD; limited characterization of when/why the CoT hacking problem arises; missing analysis of performance trade-offs when detecting hacking
Computational overhead (2× inference for counterfactuals) is understated; claimed to be 'minimal' but no actual runtime comparisons provided; at scale this could be significant yet is not quantified
BiasQA setting limitations: replacing profession with 'person' is a crude counterfactual that may not capture subtle, implicit gender biases in LLM training
Standard deviations are sometimes large (e.g., 32.5 ± 3.5), and no statistical significance testing is reported; Majority@N voting diverges from actual inference practices
